audience: undergraduate computer science; spoken explanation of 1-3 minutes

key_points.text: A process is a program in execution with its own private address space and resources (memory, open files, etc.); it is the OS's unit of isolation.
key_points.partial_if: says a process is 'a running program' without its own memory/resources

key_points.text: A thread is a unit of execution scheduled by the OS inside a process; a process has one or more threads.
key_points.partial_if: says a thread is 'part of a process' without it being the unit of execution

key_points.text: Threads of one process share its code, heap/global data and open files, but each thread has its own stack, registers and program counter.
key_points.partial_if: says threads share memory but not what each thread keeps for itself

key_points.text: Because threads share memory they communicate directly but need synchronisation (e.g. locks) to avoid race conditions; processes are isolated and communicate through IPC (pipes, sockets, shared memory), and one crashing usually does not crash another.
key_points.partial_if: mentions either the shared-memory risk or IPC, not the contrast

key_points.text: Creating and switching between threads is cheaper than for processes, because no new address space has to be set up or switched.
key_points.partial_if: says threads are 'lighter' without the reason

misconceptions.text: Each thread has its own separate memory, just like a process.
A thread and a process are the same thing, or a thread is a small separate program.
Using more threads always makes a program faster.
